text: The history of science is a long record of careful observation, bold hypothesis, and repeated correction. Early astronomers mapped the motions of the planets with remarkable precision using nothing more than the naked eye and patient tabulation. Newton later showed that a single law of gravitation could explain both the fall of an apple and the orbit of the moon, unifying the terrestrial and the celestial. In the nineteenth century, Faraday and Maxwell revealed that electricity, magnetism, and light are aspects of one electromagnetic field. Einstein then recast space and time themselves as a single flexible geometry, and quantum theory showed that nature at the smallest scales is governed by probabilities rather than certainties. Each revolution did not erase the previous one; it enlarged it, showing where the older picture remained an excellent approximation. The same pattern appears in mathematics, where new abstractions absorb old theorems as special cases, and in biology, where the discovery of DNA clarified inheritance without discarding the insights of Mendelian genetics. Progress, then, is less a matter of replacing error than of enlarging the domain in which our descriptions remain reliable, and of learning, slowly and with many mistakes, how to ask better questions of a world that does not volunteer its answers.

On the morning the train finally arrived, the station was almost empty. A thin fog clung to the platform, and the clocks disagreed with one another by a minute or two, as they always had. She had waited three winters for this, and now that the moment was here she found herself strangely calm, watching the porter load crates of apples and jars of honey into the last carriage. The conductor checked a small brass watch, frowned, and then nodded to no one in particular. Somewhere beyond the fields a bell began to ring, slow and deliberate, and the passengers who had been dozing on the benches rose one by one, gathering their coats and their questions, ready at last to go. It had rained all week, and the river beyond the embankment ran high and brown, carrying branches and the occasional white shape of a paper lantern down toward the city, where the lights were just beginning to come on along the quay.

An algorithm is a finite description of a procedure that, given an input, produces an output in a bounded number of well-defined steps. Sorting a list, finding the shortest path through a graph, and deciding whether a formula is satisfiable are all problems that can be posed in this language. Some of them admit fast solutions; others appear to require enormous effort, and the question of whether that appearance is an illusion remains one of the deepest open problems in mathematics. Complexity theory classifies problems by the resources they demand, and it has taught us to distinguish between the merely tedious and the genuinely hard. A proof that two great classes coincide, or that they do not, would reshape not only computer science but also cryptography, optimization, and much of applied mathematics. Even the everyday act of searching a list becomes, under this lens, a small illustration of a principle that governs machines and minds alike.
